Performance Testing
Our dynamic testing is performed on a closed test track. What we do there can be compartmentalized into three basic categories: straight-line performance, cornering/handling, and top speed. The heart of our test equipment is the Racelogic VBOX GPS data logger. The VBOX uses the U.S. government's GPS satellite constellation to record speed, position, and acceleration. We have various models of this data logger in our fleet, ranging from 10-Hz units (that's 10 points of data per second) to 100 Hz, and one of them even uses the Russian GLONASS satellite system in conjunction with GPS to deliver speed accuracy within 0.1 mph and positional accuracy within about six feet. Piggybacking it with a GPS base station (a device used to correct GPS positional inaccuracy) and a VBOX 3iSL (100Hz) can deliver positional accuracy to within one inch. The VBOX is what we use to measure acceleration times, braking, and top speed. Our VBOX 3i units (we have four of them) also have the ability to log vehicle data such as steering angle, engine speed, and throttle position through the vehicle's CAN communication interface.
Acceleration
Straight-line acceleration consists of three different tests: the standing start (from which we pull all the zero-to-speed times), the 5-to-60-mph rolling start, and two top-gear acceleration tests (30 to 50 mph and 50 to 70 mph). The rolling start is a C/D creation, in which we creep along at 5 mph and then accelerate as hard as possible. This test illuminates differences in powertrain flexibility. The larger the difference between a 5-to-60-mph and a zero-to-60-mph run, the more lag an engine has; this is particularly relevant today with the flurry of downsized turbocharged engines. Top-gear acceleration, in a manual-transmission car, where we simply goose the throttle and don't downshift, highlights midrange power. In a vehicle with an automatic, the transmission downshifts (and the times are much quicker), so this metric represents a combination of transmission and engine responsiveness. And that means the times between vehicles equipped with manual and automatic transmissions clearly aren't comparable.
For Sale Near You
See all results for used cars for sale near 10400
Standing start. The quarter-mile. A race from A to B. No matter what you call it, this is the test that most people care about. We test in street conditions, so launch traction is low and not the level of stick you'd find at a local drag strip. We also do not power shift, which is keeping your right foot pinned while completing a shift. It is up to the tester to determine the best launch technique, and this process can mean that some cars (for example, a launch-control-equipped Porsche 911) require just two or three launches to get the best possible time. Conventional automatics may only require five launches. High-power, rear-wheel-drive cars equipped with manual transmissions are the most time-consuming, and finding the sweet spot of balancing wheelspin and clutch engagement (usually in the 3000-to-4000-rpm range, but it varies depending on the car) may take 10 runs or more. But even with the more straightforward vehicles, we tweak our launch technique, such as by varying our brake torquing, to try to get the best possible time.
All of our straight-line acceleration results are the average of the best run in opposite directions, to account for wind. Ambient weather conditions—we record absolute barometric pressure and wet- and dry-bulb temperatures trackside—determine how much power an engine makes. Because of that, we also correct acceleration results to 60 degrees Fahrenheit at sea level. Cooler air is denser and contains more oxygen, allowing the engine to burn more fuel and make more power. Similarly, high barometric pressure produces more power than low pressure, and dry air has more oxygen than moist air. All of our standing-start acceleration times also include rollout, a short period of time (typically about 0.3 second) that we subtract from the acceleration figures. It's a phenomenon that stems from the physics of the timing lights at a drag strip, where a car can be rolling for 12 inches or more before the clock starts. We changed our procedure in 2019 to now use the industry standard 1-foot rollout and publish those rollout times for anyone wanting to compute the true zero to 60 mph time.
When possible, we also measure a vehicle's top speed. We often hit an electronic limiter during the straight-line testing, but some cars' speeds are drag limited, meaning their top speed is limited because of air resistance. Fewer cars are redline limited, meaning their top speed is reached at redline in a gear—upshift and the car can't go any faster. We don't test the top speed of every car because cars have gotten ludicrously fast in the last 20 years and we don't always have access to a safe place to do it.
Braking
Chassis performance testing answers two essential questions: how short can a car stop, and how hard can it turn. Our standard braking testing consists of six stops from 70 mph to zero. Five of them are done in close succession, with the sixth stop coming after approximately a mile of cooling so that we can roughly determine how well the brakes shed heat, which is otherwise known as "brake fade." Stopping from exactly 70.0 mph is, obviously, a very difficult thing to do. So, we stop from between 70.0 and 70.5 mph, using a tape switch on the brake pedal so we know exactly when the brake pedal is first touched. Then we correct the distance to a true 70.0-mph start with a standard calculation used throughout the automotive industry based on the average deceleration from that stop. To avoid any issues with a one-off accomplishment, we report the second-best stop from the group of six as our 70-mph-to-zero distance. On high-performance vehicles—our cutoff point is generally a quarter-mile trap speed above 100 mph—we also measure 100-mph-to-zero distance. The best sports cars wearing the highest-performance summer tires can stop from 70 mph in 140 feet or slightly less (we measured the Corvette ZR1 at 140 feet even), while heavier trucks wearing knobby off-road tires, such as the Ford F-150 Raptor R, require 200 feet or more. When you need to stop in a hurry, those additional four car lengths it takes to come to a halt can easily be the difference between an elevated heart rate and a significant collision.
Maximum Cornering (Skidpad)
Timing the lap of a car on a flat circle—we usually use a 300-foot-diameter circle, but we occasionally use a smaller circle out of necessity—allows us to calculate the average lateral acceleration of a car. We straddle the painted line that defines the circle with the vehicle's tires, do laps in both directions, and average the results, which we report as roadholding in g-force. Fun fact: Almost every car turns a faster lap in the counterclockwise direction, because the position of a driver on the inside of a car shifts less load to the stressed outside tires. Cornering results range from 0.63 g for a Mercedes-Benz G-class to nearly double that for the grippiest sports cars.
Test-Vehicle Prep
Just like any other researchers conducting a controlled case study, we use a specific procedure for our test vehicles. Before a vehicle can hit the test track, it must undergo numerous prepping protocols, ensuring that every vehicle's performance is measured on a level playing field. By taking these measures, we can consistently yield accurate real-world results and confidently compare data from a recent test to one from years back.
From start to finish, the prep process is very thorough. All the information is recorded on a template called a track sheet. When the test is completed, the track sheet's data is stored in our database where it will live on for eternity as reference material. First, the vehicle is carefully topped off with fuel and weighed using our Intercomp wireless scales. The corresponding weight of each corner is then recorded on the track sheet. This is where the total weight, as well as front and rear weight distribution, will be calculated and recorded.
Next, a technical assistant scrutinizes every detail of the vehicle, both inside and out. During this inspection, numerous data points are captured and recorded on the track sheet, such as engine layout (front, mid, or rear), driven wheels (front, rear, or all-wheel drive), transmission type, steering wheel turns from lock to lock, and tire specifications. Correctly recording the tire information is a crucial aspect of prepping a car for the track because tires influence nearly all performance metrics, including cornering grip, braking, and launch traction. Not only must the name, size, and any manufacturer-specific markings be noted, but the tires must also be set to the manufacturer's recommended cold-tire-pressure specification, which is located on the vehicle's door placard or in the owner's manual. Finally, the engine oil level is checked to ensure that it is at the recommended level. When all procedures have been completed, the vehicle is finally track ready. With a rich history rooted in instrumented testing, we take great pride in publishing test data that is honest, accurate, and dependable.
Interior Sound Level
While at the test track measuring performance, we also use a Brüel & Kjær 2250-L Class 1 sound meter to measure the sound-pressure level in each car under three different conditions: at idle, while accelerating at wide-open-throttle to 70 mph, and at a steady 70-mph cruise. Each car is tested on the same section of road to ensure the results are comparable, since the road surface has a significant impact on the noise level inside a vehicle. In 2025, we started reporting the results from the idle and 70-mph cruise measurements in sones as well as the traditional A-weighted decibels that we've used for decades. Sones are a unit that was created using a panel of judges to better equate it to how the human ear perceives sound. It's also a linear scale, which makes it far more straightforward to interpret comparisons between vehicles than decibels' logarithmic scale.
Fuel Economy and Driving Range
All light-duty vehicles are required by law to have their fuel-economy estimates certified by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). These city, highway, and combined ratings are boldly listed on new vehicles' window stickers and often used by manufacturers as advertisement fodder. Plug-in hybrids and electric vehicles also receive estimates for electric operation. Expressed in MPGe, these estimates are intended to be an easy way to compare the efficiency of an electric to a gasoline-powered car on an energy-equivalent basis. But there is a drawback to using EPA numbers that few people realize: the agency actually does very few of its own tests. Surprise! The EPA lists ratings that are mostly self-reported by auto manufacturers. Whether the testing is performed by the automaker or the EPA, they are done inside on a sort-of treadmill for vehicles that eliminates variables such as temperature and traffic. These scientific methods provide the best way to directly compare two vehicles. However, the EPA tests are not necessarily indicative of how people drive in the real world, and the test cycles don't include speeds as low as what's experienced in areas of dense traffic or high as those that tend to be driven on U.S. highways. That's why we created our own uniform highway fuel-economy test.
Highway Fuel-Economy Test
We run all our tests at a GPS-verified 75 mph on a 200-mile out-and-back loop on the highways that surround our Michigan headquarters. Our consistent procedure includes a methodical fill-up process, following a specific route, using cruise control, and setting the climate control to the same temperature (72 degrees auto). We also correct for odometer error, and we don't test in heavy wind or rain or with extra passengers. In the event we encounter too much traffic or unusual conditions, we abort the run and try again later.
We follow the same procedure for electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids, except for these, we have additional steps that include making sure the battery is fully charged before starting and recording the battery state of charge and predicted range values every five miles, and then the kilowatt-hours (kWh) needed to fill the battery after the drive loop. Plug-in hybrids also get a highway EV range and MPGe economy for those miles. MPGe is calculated just like miles per gallon of gas only using the EPA's equivalence factor of 1 gallon = 33.7 kWh of electricity to arrive at the result. For plug-ins that can't hit 75 mph in electric mode, we instead first drain the battery and then start the test in charge-sustaining (hybrid) mode. Since those plug-ins don't use any electricity, their results are in miles per gallon rather than MPGe. Likewise, we have to shorten our route for EVs that don't have the range to complete the entire loop. We still give them an MPGe number, though.
Highway Driving Range
The highway range figure we report is the maximum distance that a vehicle can travel at 75 mph on a full tank of gas. We take the fuel economy from our highway test and multiply it by the vehicle's fuel-tank capacity. For example, the six-cylinder Mazda CX-90 averaged 30 mpg on our fuel loop and has a 19.6-gallon tank. This equates to an impressive 588 miles of range, but we round down to the nearest 10-mile increment and publish it as 580 miles. That's because when it comes to something that can strand you by the side of the road, we believe it's better to publish conservative figures rather than distances that are more difficult to achieve. A range figure under about 400 miles is the threshold where fill ups can become annoyingly frequent.
Our process is different for electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids. For plug-ins, we simply note how many miles we get into our loop before the battery runs out of juice and the vehicle switches on the internal-combustion engine. EVs are more complicated, because as the battery charge gets really low they generally can't maintain highway speed and tend to go into a low-speed limp mode. (Plus, then we'd be stranded on the side of the highway.) And we also can't calculate range based on the energy put back into the pack after a test, because that would include the inefficiencies of the charging process. So we use our log of estimated range and battery state of charge from the trip computer every five miles. We then plot all of those points and fit a curve to project out to our range figure, again rounding down to the nearest 10-mile increment.
Observed Fuel Economy
To give consumers an idea of how efficient a vehicle is in mixed driving conditions, we track all fill-ups and mileage on our test vehicles. We do the same with electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids, except for those we track electrical energy (kWh) instead of gallons of fuel. This information is documented for every model that is part of a comparison, long-term, or instrumented test. However, we eliminate the miles recorded during track testing and during our highway fuel loop. We also ensure that every odometer reading is accurate to create a level playing field for all the cars we test.
The observed fuel-economy number we publish has variables such as driving style (our staffers have heavier feet than most consumers, and some more than others) and distance traveled. This means that comparing the economy of one tested vehicle to another can be imperfect except for in our comparison tests, for which all the cars are driven the same distances and in the same conditions. So we consider our observed mpg as supplementary to the EPA estimates and the results of our real-world highway fuel-economy test.
Cargo Space and Storage
The car-shopping process is both rewarding and exhausting, sometimes even frustrating. People spend countless hours between dealerships and websites narrowing down body styles, drivetrains, brands, and features. While only you can decide between black and beige leather, we can take the heavy lifting out of your car-shopping experience—literally. We measure every nook and cranny inside the vehicle so that we can compare cargo and storage space with its peers and so that you know which vehicle is going to fit the most hockey bags, tool boxes, or Costco pallets before you even set foot on a dealer lot.
Carry-Ons
Manufacturers provide scientifically measured cargo-volume numbers that adhere to engineering standards, but those figures can vary depending on which version of that standard the automaker is measuring to. These numbers are also difficult to translate into real-world practicality. If Honda states that the Civic hatchback has 25 cubic feet of space in its trunk, how do you know if that's enough space to get your in-laws and their stuff home from the airport? C/D's testing showed that the Civic hatchback can fit six pieces of standard carry-on luggage with all seats up, a figure that we think is easier to visualize.
To perform this test, we use cardboard boxes measuring 9.0 by 14.0 by 22.0 inches, which are the maximum dimensions for carry-on luggage allowed by many major U.S. airlines. Starting from the front row, we begin by moving the front seats to the minimum comfortable setting for a person that's 5'10" tall. Without removing anything we deem necessary for safe travel (headrests, spare tires, first aid kits), we fill the rearmost cargo area (either a sedan's trunk or the cargo area behind an SUV's or minivan's second or third row) with carry-on boxes, attempting to fit as many boxes as possible in the space. After reaching a maximum, we close the space, ensuring that the trunk or liftgate closes without interference—we will not force the door closed or bend any boxes. After the maximum capacity has been recorded, we fold the second and third rows and repeat. If seats fold in multiple ways (some cars have stowable seat bottoms, for example), we will determine the configuration that allows the maximum number of boxes. As with the trunk, all doors must close without interference. For models with various trims, we only retest vehicles with substantial differences in cargo area—such as those with a hybrid battery or a different seating configuration. For pickup trucks, we only test the enclosed space. Our current champ is a Ford Transit Cargo Van with 188 boxes, while a C8 Corvette Stingray holds just one in its front trunk.
Ping-Pong Balls
Have you ever situated yourself in a new car only find out that there isn't enough space for your phone, sunglasses, wallet, makeup, snacks, purse, and napkins? It's difficult to estimate how one car's interior storage space compares to another's. This is why we devised our ping-pong-ball test. By filling interior storage pockets with ping-pong balls, we can objectively show how vehicles measure up to their competitors.
To perform this test, we remove everything from the cubby, such as owner's manuals or removable storage trays, as these could reasonably be relocated should an owner need to maximize a particular storage space. For open bins, we add ping-pong balls arranged at random until the bin or cubby is full. An open cubby is considered full when the balls reach a level where no ball is more than halfway above the top edge. For closed compartments such as the glovebox or center console, the enclosure must be able to latch closed with no resistance from the ping-pong balls. At that point, the total number of balls is recorded. Every defined storage space in the vehicle is counted, including door pockets and underfloor spaces but excluding seatback map pockets and door handles that fit less than six balls.
Lift-Over Height
While high seating positions and ride heights are all the rage, they often bring high cargo openings. We measure this height—to the nearest tenth of an inch—to show how high an object must be lifted in order to place it in a trunk or cargo area. For sedans this usually means the middle of the trunk lip, and for SUVs and hatchbacks this typically means the carpeted part of the load floor. If a vehicle has an adjustable suspension with a loading or parked setting, we will test at both heights. When testing pickup trucks, we measure to the surface of the open tailgate.
Visibility and Seating Height
In an automotive market experiencing the rapid proliferation of the crossover as well as the resurgence of trucks and SUVs, seating height has never been a more scrutinized metric. As people continue gravitating toward larger vehicles with higher seating heights, this measurement—which we determine by measuring the distance from the driver's hip-point (or H-point) to the ground—will undoubtedly become increasingly important to prospective buyers.
Simply put, the H-point is the theoretical location of an occupant's hip joint in a vehicle's seat, and it's determined using the SAE International engineering organization's aptly named H-point machine (HPM). The HPM is a plastic and steel human-shaped device designed to mimic a 50th-percentile male (69.1 inches tall and weighing 172 pounds). The H-point could be considered the starting point when designing an interior, because it influences many aspects such as roof height, seating height, collision performance, outward visibility, interior packaging, and even the door apertures.
To find the H-point of a car, we set the driver's seat to the middle of its vertical and horizontal travel, giving us a consistent location from which to start each of our tests. Next, the HPM is assembled in the seat. Once the HPM is settled and level, it indicates the H-point with crosshairs located on the side of the device. We verify seating height using a floor jack and a laser level, by lining up the laser with the crosshairs and a level yardstick. It is interesting to note that the H-points of a segment usually fall within a fairly tight range—usually within one to three inches of each other,—except for the SUV and truck segments, where it can be as much as five to 10 inches.
The HPM is a highly versatile instrument; besides its obvious use for locating the H-point, we also use it to measure outward visibility. By mounting a laser to the "head" of the HPM, we measure the horizontal obstruction of each roof pillar in relation to the driver's sightline, measured in degrees. We subtract the obstructed portions from 360 degrees, allowing us to calculate the amount of unobstructed outward visibility.
We also measure how much of the roadway in front of and behind the vehicle is obscured by the car itself. First we measure the distance in feet that is blocked by the hood, then we make the same measurement in feet for how much of the roadway can't be seen when looking over the trunk or hatch through the rearview mirror. The results aren't always intuitive and are heavily dependent on the vehicle's styling. For example, the Honda Accord has an abnormally long obscured rear view of 138 feet (the Camry's is half as much), while a Mercedes-Benz G550 has only 31 feet blocked to the rear because it is more upright and doesn't have a trunk protruding off the back of the vehicle.
Center-of-Gravity Height
A car's center of gravity (CG) is the hypothetical point in a vehicle that is equivalent to the average location of all of the masses of the individual components, and it's important because it directly influences a car's dynamic traits. The lower it is, the better. A low CG reduces the load transfer when cornering and thus limits body roll while improving transient behavior. Beyond the implications for ride quality and handling, it also reduces the possibility of a rollover incident. Low-slung sports cars, which are painstakingly engineered to carry the majority of their weight very low to the ground, generally have a very stable and confident feeling through corners, whereas SUVs and tall trucks tend to exhibit more body roll and can feel tippy in the same situations.
To calculate the CG, we first measure the height of the wheel centers and weigh the vehicle using four individual scales (one per wheel) on a perfectly level floor. We calculate the longitudinal location of the center of gravity using the static weight distribution and the wheelbase (the distance between the front and rear axles). The heaviest axle of the car is then lifted and positioned on blocks, which are 17.9 inches tall, and the non-lifted axle is weighed again.
The increase in the weight on the static axle provides the critical variable to solving a trigonometric equation that determines the height of the vehicle's center of gravity. For the mathematically minded, we've detailed this in more advanced language here.
It should be noted that we don’t measure the center-of-gravity height for every vehicle we review. We generally perform this test on performance-oriented cars, as this type of data is of greater interest for them than for mainstream sedans, crossovers, and pickup trucks.
Safety and Warranty
Safety is one of the few areas in which C/D relies on outside testing to inform our ratings. Two agencies, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS), perform crash tests on cars in the United States. The ratings those agencies produce, which are found on window stickers in dealerships across the country, form the backbone of our safety ratings. When a car hasn't yet been tested by either agency, we don't assign it a safety rating.
That's not to say that we don't perform our own subjective evaluations of available safety equipment. When cars are equipped with active-safety technologies, we leave them engaged during our test drives and note whether they perform well or are intrusive. We also keep a rear-facing infant seat handy to test out the ease of child-seat installation in any given car. We're checking to see how easy it is to access LATCH anchors, whether there's space for a rear-facing seat behind a comfortably adjusted front seat, and whether the child seat sits level without the aid of bolsters or other extra equipment. Finally, we collect data on the availability of a spare tire and evaluate backup-camera operation.
Taken with the crash-test data, all of this information helps to provide a picture not only of a car's safety credentials, but also of how easy it is for buyers to opt into a model with desirable features. Safety is one of only a few categories in which our ratings are given on an absolute scale rather than determined in relation to a vehicle's direct competitors. If a compact sedan needs nine seconds to reach 60 mph but tracks closely with its key rivals, we won't knock it in our ratings. But a poor crash test result is bad news, even if the competition performs similarly.
Warranty
Most of the cars we test come to us as loans from automakers, so there's not much room to test the practical benefits of any given warranty. However, our long-term test cars, which stay in our stables for 40,000 miles, provide an opportunity to become acquainted with the coverage and service offered by various brands. To rate warranties, we compare the lengths of coverage periods and note whether extras such as regularly scheduled maintenance are included or whether there is a hybrid-specific warranty. We typically award the highest ratings to cars with the longest coverage periods and deduct points when a company falls short of its direct competitors or fails to offer a feature that others in its class provide.
Overall Ratings
When compiling our reviews, we assign ratings on a ten-point scale to every car, truck, and SUV. In general, we determine the ratings based on the car's results in our extensive testing, but also based on our subjective evaluations after driving and spending time in the car.
We evaluate a car only in comparison to its competitors. We won't knock a minivan for needing more time to complete a quarter-mile than a supercar does, for instance. A hybrid that earns 40 mpg on the highway may be derided, while a crossover will earn praise for topping 30 mpg. In certain instances, though, we rate cars based on the overall market. Poor crash-test scores, for instance, are not overlooked simply because the rest of the class has also struggled. Because opinions can vary among our staff, we discuss (argue) before a core team finalizes them, to ensure that no rogue opinions can unfairly raise or tank a vehicle's score.
Dave VanderWerp has spent more than 20 years in the automotive industry, in varied roles from engineering to product consulting, and now leading Car and Driver's vehicle-testing efforts. Dave got his very lucky start at C/D by happening to submit an unsolicited resume at just the right time to land a part-time road warrior job when he was a student at the University of Michigan, where he immediately became enthralled with the world of automotive journalism.

title: Looking for the Right SUV? Start with the Best of 2026
text:
If you're a new car buyer, chances are an SUV is on your shopping list. And if that's the case, you're spoiled for choice. Whether you're looking for a subcompact or full-size model, or anything in between, SUVs exist at pretty much every price point imaginable and in every shape, size, and powertrain configuration you can think of.
Here, we've ranked the best SUVs in every segment based on roughly 200 data points encompassing acceleration, handling, comfort, cargo space, fuel efficiency, value, and how enjoyable they are to drive. Car and Driver's rankings are arrived at from the results of our extensive instrumented testing of several hundred vehicles each year and from our expert editors' subjective impressions gained in real-world driving. We take rankings seriously because we want you to know everything about the vehicles that you're interested in.
C/D SAYS: The Honda CR-V is one of the most recognizable compact SUVs on the planet, and with an agreeable ride and a spacious interior, it's also one of the best.Learn More
C/D SAYS: While you can't remove its roof or doors—like you can with the big, bad Bronco—the 2026 Ford Bronco Sport can get further out into the boonies than many rivals. Learn More
C/D SAYS: The Chevrolet Trax is one of the least expensive new cars on the market, but its quality construction and pleasant driving experience are a step above its asking price.Learn More
C/D SAYS: A near-luxury interior and plenty of behind-the-wheel verve set the Mazda CX-30 apart from its subcompact SUV rivals, but its small cabin hampers utility.Learn More
C/D SAYS: The 2026 Kia Seltos SUV is relatively efficient and affordable but not terribly engaging, putting it somewhere in the middle of the crowded subcompact-SUV segment.Learn More
C/D SAYS: The mid-size 2026 Hyundai Palisade SUV Hybrid makes its debut sharing the same all-new boxy styling and premium feature updates as the nonhybrid model.Learn More
C/D SAYS: Building on its proven three-row electric SUV, the EV9 ramps up the excitement for 2026 with a new high-performance GT model aiming to break 500 horsepower. Learn More

C/D SAYS: The 2026 Buick Envista subcompact SUV offers youthful, contemporary styling and an efficient powertrain at a remarkably affordable price. Learn More
C/D SAYS: The Honda CR-V is one of the most recognizable compact SUVs on the planet, and with an agreeable ride and a spacious interior, it's also one of the best.Learn More
C/D SAYS: The 2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid takes the inherent goodness of the CR-V compact SUV and adds a polished hybrid powertrain for increased efficiency and performance.Learn More
C/D SAYS: With decent range, fast charging, and a spacious interior, the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 EV is a versatile tool for navigating modern life.Learn More
C/D SAYS: The 2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid takes the inherent goodness of the CR-V compact SUV and adds a polished hybrid powertrain for increased efficiency and performance.Learn More
C/D SAYS: With decent range, fast charging, and a spacious interior, the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 EV is a versatile tool for navigating modern life.Learn More
SUV stands for 'sport utility vehicle,' a term that originated from the definition of these models as recreational-use vehicles for off-roading with extra utility when compared with a sedan or a pickup truck. In more descriptive terms, SUVs are vehicles that have generous interior space and cargo capacity, perform well in a variety of different driving environments, and ride higher than sedans while, in many cases, still delivering car-like handling. That combination of characteristics has made SUVs the most popular type of vehicle in the United States.
As a blend between a sedan and a truck, the benefits of SUVs are that they can be versatile, comfortable, and practical—all at the same time. While modern SUVs are generally more comfort-focused than they used to be, many still offer reasonable off-road and towing capabilities. Many people buy SUVs for family transportation, as they can generally carry up to five passengers comfortably. Some mid-size and most full-size SUVs also offer three-row seating, which can accommodate an additional two or three people.
There are many different kinds of SUVs, as they come in many shapes and sizes ranging from station-wagon-like crossovers to massive truck-based three-row luxury land yachts. Subcompact and compact crossovers and SUVs are the smallest breeds and can offer a bit more versatility and interior space than a sedan. Mid-size SUVs are the next step up in size, providing significantly more interior space, higher cargo capacities, and often the option of third-row seating. Full-size SUVs are the largest, offering the roomiest interiors, the most cargo capacity, and the highest tow ratings. There's quite a bit of variability within those segments, as some SUVs are designed for off-road prowess, while others prioritize luxury and comfort.
C/D SAYS: If towing is on the task list, but you also need to haul up to nine people and their cargo simultaneously, the 2026 Chevy Suburban is the SUV best suited to the job. Learn More
C/D SAYS: The 2026 Chevy Tahoe is as refined on the road as it is capable off-road, and its variety of use cases makes it an attractive option among full-size SUVs. Learn More
C/D SAYS: With the power and capacity to move eight people, their gear, and a trailer with ease, the 2026 GMC Yukon SUV is a true utility vehicle. Learn More
C/D SAYS: The Tesla Model Y receives a significant refresh for 2026, which keeps the popular electric SUV in the hunt among a growing segment of attractive options.Learn More
C/D SAYS: The 2026 Mitsubishi Outlander Hybrid is relatively competent and efficient but feels a little dated in the face of more modern competitors.Learn More
C/D SAYS: Redesigned for 2026, the RAV4 Hybrid and RAV4 Plug-in Hybrid models are new, improved, and ready to take on our favorite compact SUVs.Learn More
C/D SAYS: The 2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid takes the inherent goodness of the CR-V compact SUV and adds a polished hybrid powertrain for increased efficiency and performance.Learn More
C/D SAYS: The 2026 Hyundai Tucson Hybrid SUV doesn't cost much more than its nonhybrid sibling but offers better fuel efficiency and quicker acceleration. Learn More
C/D SAYS: The Sportage Hybrid is a roomy, comfortable, and practical SUV, but we expected better fuel efficiency from its hybrid powertrains. Learn More

C/D SAYS: For the second generation of its popular Telluride SUV, Kia has added a hybrid variant with more power and better fuel economy than the standard model. Learn More
C/D SAYS: The 2026 Toyota Grand Highlander Hybrid SUV is bigger inside than the standard Highlander and offers a satisfyingly strong powertrain not available on the shorter version.Learn More
C/D SAYS: Decent, affordable transportation like the 2026 Toyota Corolla Cross Hybrid is becoming a rarity, but if you want more excitement you'll need to look elsewhere. Learn More
C/D SAYS: The 2026 Mercedes-Benz GLC-Class Hybrid SUV is a plug-in that can go an impressive 54 miles on electricity alone, but it's not as impressive when the charge runs out. Learn More
C/D SAYS: Read our 2026 Volvo XC60 Hybrid review for information on ratings, pricing, specs, and features, and see how this SUV performed in our testing. Learn More
C/D SAYS: The 2026 Hyundai Tucson Hybrid SUV doesn't cost much more than its nonhybrid sibling but offers better fuel efficiency and quicker acceleration. Learn More
C/D SAYS: The 2026 Cayenne E-Hybrid is Porsche’s attempt at distilling nearly 80 years' worth of sports car pedigree into a plug-in-hybrid SUV — and it mostly works. Learn More
C/D SAYS: The BMW X5 Hybrid brings all the luxury and sportiness of the regular X5 with a plug-in hybrid powertrain for increased fuel efficiency.Learn More
C/D SAYS: The 2026 Lexus NX lacks the playful character of some subcompact SUV competitors, but its quiet, smooth ride and upscale interior delight. Learn More
C/D SAYS: For the 2026 model year, the Nissan Leaf EV is reimagined as a small SUV with more modern styling, better range, and a nicer interior.Learn More
C/D SAYS: The 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 N is as successful in pushing the envelope of EV performance as it is in mimicking the driving experience of an internal-combustion vehicle. Learn More
C/D SAYS: With decent range, fast charging, and a spacious interior, the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 EV is a versatile tool for navigating modern life.Learn More
C/D SAYS: Building on its proven three-row electric SUV, the EV9 ramps up the excitement for 2026 with a new high-performance GT model aiming to break 500 horsepower. Learn More
C/D SAYS: The Trailseeker joins Subaru's EV lineup, sporting some off-road capability and dressed in a mid-size SUV body with lifted station-wagon proportions. Learn More
C/D SAYS: The 2026 Volvo XC40 is a strong contender among subcompact luxury SUVs thanks to its youthful, clean design and generous feature set.Learn More
C/D SAYS: The 2026 BMW X1 is an excellent subcompact SUV for anyone who values driving as much as they do a tech-forward, luxurious interior. Learn More
C/D SAYS: Just as the 911 is a benchmark sports car, the Porsche Macan is a high-water mark for athletic compact crossovers that others look up to. Learn More
C/D SAYS: The GV70 achieves luxury-SUV superstardom thanks to athletic dynamics and a knockout design, and the 2026 model brings an enhanced interior and design tweaks.Learn More
C/D SAYS: For Lucid's second act, the EV startup has rolled out the 2026 Gravity SUV, with an upscale cabin and a maximum estimated range of 450 miles per charge.Learn More
C/D SAYS: The Honda CR-V is one of the most recognizable compact SUVs on the planet, and with an agreeable ride and a spacious interior, it's also one of the best.Learn More

For more than 60 years we've been answering the objective questions—How fast? How quick? How much grip?—comprehensively, and with an authority based in experience that our readers have come to rely on. Read on for the full details on how we collect more than 200 data points on the roughly 400 vehicles that we test every year.
Dave VanderWerp has spent more than 20 years in the automotive industry, in varied roles from engineering to product consulting, and now leading Car and Driver's vehicle-testing efforts.

title: Is a BMW X5 Extended Warranty Worth It? Full Breakdown of Plans and Pricing
author: Horatiu Boeriu
text:
The BMW X5 is known for its luxury, performance, and advanced technology, but maintaining a high-end vehicle like this can become expensive as it ages. That’s where an extended warranty can play a crucial role. Understanding the costs, coverage, and available plans for a BMW X5 extended warranty can help you make a more informed decision on protecting your investment. Here’s a comprehensive guide to the BMW X5 extended warranty options.
What Is an Extended Warranty?
An extended warranty is a service agreement that offers coverage beyond the original manufacturer’s warranty. While BMW’s factory warranty typically lasts for 4 years or 50,000 miles, an extended warranty can add years of protection, covering mechanical breakdowns, electrical components, and even certain high-tech features. This gives you peace of mind, knowing that unexpected repair costs won’t derail your budget.
Want a Warranty Now? Exclusive BMWBLOG Offers on Third-Party Warranties
Don’t need additional research and just need a warranty now? We’ve partnered with industry leaders, offering discounted rates for BMWBLOG patrons. CARCHEX is one of the most reputable extended warranty providers in the business, and we’re proud to offer $100 off with CARCHEX. Just follow the “Get Quote” buttons below!
If you need to get a quote immediately, you can read more about our partners at CARCHEX!
Disclaimer: This post contains affiliate links. If you use these links to buy something we may earn a commission. Thank you.
Third-Party Extended Warranty Options: Cost and Benefits
While BMW’s extended warranty options are compelling, they come with certain limitations. For instance, coverage is only valid when the vehicle is serviced at a BMW dealership, which isn’t always convenient. Plus, these warranties tend to be more expensive, and not every BMW X5 is eligible depending on age and mileage.
Using a third-party warranty, such as CARCHEX, can be a cost-effective solution. These providers often offer extended coverage up to ten years and include a lower deductible, keeping repair costs more manageable. Many third-party warranties eliminate mileage restrictions altogether or extend coverage up to the 250,000-mile mark!
Key Benefits of Third-Party Warranties:
- Lower Cost: Typically, third-party options are more affordable than manufacturer-backed warranties.
- Longer Coverage Periods: Some plans last up to 10 years, significantly longer than BMW’s extended warranty.
- High Mileage Options: Coverage is often available for vehicles with high mileage, which may not qualify for BMW’s plans.
- Customizable Tiers: Just like BMW’s structure, third-party providers offer multiple levels of coverage, so you can choose a plan that fits your needs.
- Additional Perks: Many third-party warranties include towing, rental car reimbursement, and even roadside assistance.
Things to Consider Before Purchasing a Third-Party Warranty
One aspect to note is the “waiting period” associated with many third-party warranties. During this introductory period (usually around 30 days and 1,000 miles), claims may not be covered. This is an industry-standard practice meant to prevent fraudulent claims, but it’s worth considering if you’re close to needing repairs. Therefore, it’s always in your best interest to get coverage sooner rather than later.
BMW X5 Extended Warranty Plans
BMW offers extended warranty plans under the umbrella of BMW Extended Service Contracts, which are available at any BMW dealership. These plans are customizable and cater to various needs, offering up to 7 years or 100,000 miles of coverage. BMW provides three primary levels of protection:
1. Platinum Protection
The Platinum plan is BMW’s most comprehensive extended warranty. It covers almost every part of the vehicle, including the powertrain, electrical components, suspension, steering, brakes, air conditioning, high-tech systems, and even some interior trim pieces. This plan is ideal for drivers who want nearly complete coverage and are looking to keep their BMW X5 in like-new condition for as long as possible.
What’s Covered:
- Engine and Transmission
- Suspension and Steering
- Fuel and Cooling System
- Brakes (excluding wear items like pads and rotors)
- HVAC systems
- Navigation, audio, and high-tech electronics
- Safety and restraint systems
Cost: The Platinum plan typically costs between $5,000 and $7,000, depending on the vehicle’s age, mileage, and location.
2. Gold Protection
The Gold plan is a mid-level option that covers most major components but excludes some non-essential systems like navigation, entertainment, and convenience features. It’s a good choice for drivers who want to keep their BMW X5 running smoothly without paying for premium-level coverage.
What’s Covered:
- Engine and Transmission
- Drive Axles
- Suspension and Steering
- Electrical systems
- Cooling and Fuel Systems
Cost: Expect to pay between $3,500 and $5,500 for this level of coverage.
3. Powertrain Plus
The Powertrain Plus plan is BMW’s most basic extended warranty option, focusing solely on the essential mechanical parts such as the engine, transmission, and drive components. It doesn’t cover electrical systems, safety technology, or luxury features, making it more affordable but less comprehensive.
What’s Covered:
- Engine
- Transmission
- Drive Axles
Cost: Pricing ranges from $2,000 to $3,500, depending on the vehicle’s mileage and age.
Additional Coverage Options
BMW X5 owners can also add optional coverage for specific components or services, depending on their needs:
- Tire and Wheel Protection: Covers damage to tires and wheels due to road hazards.
- Ding and Dent Repair: Repairs minor dents and dings without affecting your X5’s factory paint.
- Key Replacement: Replaces lost or damaged keys, which can be costly for modern BMWs.
These options can be added individually, giving you a more tailored approach to your warranty.
Factors Affecting Extended Warranty Cost
Several factors can influence the cost of an extended warranty for the BMW X5:
- Vehicle Age and Mileage: Newer vehicles with lower mileage will generally cost less to cover than older, high-mileage models.
- Coverage Length: Longer warranty periods (e.g., 7 years/100,000 miles) will naturally be more expensive than shorter terms (e.g., 5 years/75,000 miles).
- Location: Warranty prices can vary depending on the region due to differences in labor rates and repair costs.
- Deductible Choice: Choosing a lower deductible (e.g., $0 or $50) will increase the overall cost of the warranty compared to a higher deductible ($200+).
Is an Extended Warranty Worth It for a BMW X5?
The BMW X5 is a complex vehicle, featuring high-performance powertrains, sophisticated all-wheel-drive systems, and numerous tech features that can be expensive to repair. Extended warranties are often seen as a wise investment, particularly for those planning to keep their BMW X5 beyond its factory warranty period.
For example, a single engine repair on a BMW X5 can cost upwards of $5,000, while transmission repairs or replacements might run between $4,000 and $8,000. Even replacing some of the vehicle’s advanced electrical systems can cost several thousand dollars. Given these potential costs, an extended warranty may pay for itself with just one or two major repairs.
Where to Buy an Extended Warranty for a BMW X5
BMW offers extended warranties through their authorized dealerships, which means you’ll need to visit your local BMW dealer to purchase one. However, it’s worth noting that you can also explore third-party warranty providers, which sometimes offer more flexible terms or lower pricing. Some reputable third-party options include CARCHEX!

title: BMW Extended Warranty: Is It Worth It? (2026)
author: Horatiu Boeriu
text:
Table of contents
Quick Summary:
- BMW Extended Warranty Cost: $3,000–$6,000
- Third-Party Coverage (CARCHEX): Often cheaper, more flexible
- Best For: Owners keeping their BMWs 3+ years or outside original warranty
- Top Tip: Extended warranties can easily pay for themselves with one major repair.
Is your BMW’s factory warranty nearing its end? In this comprehensive guide for 2026, we navigate the world of extended warranties, specifically designed to keep your BMW running smoothly and protect your wallet from unforeseen repair costs. A BMW Extended Warranty plan provides comprehensive coverage beyond the factory warranty, ensuring peace of mind and best value for your prized BMW.
We’ll delve into the coverage options offered by two BMW extended warranty plans, empowering you to make an informed decision. But wait, there’s more! We’ll also shed light on third-party warranty providers, exploring their potential advantages and helping you weigh all your options. Finally, we’ll unveil our top picks for the best BMW extended car warranty companies, ensuring you find the perfect fit for your BMW and driving needs. There is also a discount included!
I Need An Extended Warranty Now!
Don’t need additional research and just need a warranty now? We’ve partnered with two industry leaders, offering discounted rates for BMWBLOG patrons. CARCHEX is one of the most reputable extended warranty providers in the business, and we’re proud to offer $100 off with CARCHEX. Just follow the “Get Quote” buttons below!
If you still need additional guidance or want to do some more research, read on. You can read more about our partners at CARCHEX here!
Disclaimer: This post contains affiliate links. If you use these links to buy something we may earn a commission. Thank you.
Is The Extended Maintenance Warranty Worth It?
BMWs are beautiful and luxurious cars. Unfortunately, that entails luxury running costs. Even routine maintenance for a BMW can be considerably more expensive than some buyers are prepared for. And if you plan to keep your car for more than a couple years, it’s definitely a good idea to keep your BMW maintained by the experts. Deferred maintenance can eventually add up to huge repair costs.
Here are some examples of cost associated with repairs out of warranty:
2018 BMW 740i
- Brakes – all four corners: $2500
- Oil service: $129
- Fuel pump replacement: $2750
- Battery + alternator: $550 + $2980
2018 BMW X3 xDrive30i
- Brakes – all four corners: $1850
- Oil service: $119
- Fuel pump replacement: $1425
- Battery + alternator: $449 + $1675
2018 BMW 230i Coupe
- Brakes – all four corners: $1750
- Oil service: $119
- Fuel pump replacement: $1425
- Battery + alternator: $449 + $1890
In almost any case, it makes sense to buy an extended warranty if you can answer yes to either or both of the following questions. First – did you buy a pre-owned BMW? And second – do plan on keeping your BMW for longer than a couple years?
Extended warranties offer a lot of peace of mind and can save you thousands of dollars – it’s worth looking into them!
Extended Warranty Cost and Length
BMW offers many competitively priced and customizable extended warranties. While fairly comprehensive, there are some limitations that may exclude you from being eligible. The general exclusions are as follows:
- Cars older than model year 2017
- Vehicles over 60,000 miles
- A vehicle with an in-service date of over 3 years ago, and not already covered under UltimateCare +
For demonstration purposes, let’s use a 2019 X3 with 30,000 miles. BMW’s own website touts Ultimate Care +4 as covering up to 7 years/125,000 miles for $4699. When you consider the average BMW costs between $1000 and $1700 each year to maintain, it seems like a no brainer.
More expensive cars – think, a 7 Series or an M3 – can cost a bit more than that $4699. But the parts are much more expensive, and typically the jobs require more labor time. Expect to pay up to $8,000 for the maximum BMW extended warranty on an expensive vehicle. It is still highly likely that an extended warranty will save you hundreds or even thousands of dollars. Amazingly, a third-party warranty might be able to save you even more!
Of course, if you don’t need coverage that long, BMW makes it easy because Ultimate Care is tiered. Ultimate Care+ is the entry-level extension, costing under $1000 for most models and additionally covering brakes, wipers, and clutches. Coverage is easy to extend or cancel, and totally transferable.
Third Party Extended Warranty Cost and Length
While BMW’s extended warranty options are compelling, there are downsides. First of all, you’re only able to service the vehicle at a BMW dealership – not always convenient. Though the potential to save money is there, they are still very expensive. And of course, many vehicles are simply not eligible.
Using a third-party warranty, such as CARCHEX, is generally less expensive and can in some cases cover a longer term than BMW’s warranty options. Many offer terms up to ten years, and usually feature a very low deductible, further keeping repair costs manageable. Mileage is another aspect that is often capped, and many third-party companies either do away with mileage restrictions completely or cover cars even up to the 250,000 mile mark!
Most third-party warranties also adopt a “tier” structure like BMW, offering even further customizability. These will also feature add-ons; some popular ones are free towing, rental car reimbursements, and even roadside assistance!
One thing to note: many third-party companies have a “waiting” period, or introductory period. Claims are generally not covered during this period (commonly around 30 days and 1,000 miles). So it’s always in your best interest to get covered sooner, rather than later.
BMW Extended Warranty Comparison Chart
This table highlights the key differences between BMW’s own extended warranty and two popular third-party options—CARCHEX.
| Feature | BMW Warranty | CARCHEX | ENDURANCE | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Max Coverage Length | Up to 7 years | Up to 10 years | Up to 10 years | 
| Eligible Miles | 50,000 miles | Up to 250,000 miles | Unlimited | 
| Can Use Non-BMW Shops | No | Yes | Yes | 
| Roadside Assistance | No | Yes | Yes | 
| Transferable | Yes | Yes | Yes | 
| Estimated Cost Range | $3,000-$6,000 | $2,000-$4,500 | $2,000-$5,000 | 
BMW New Vehicle Limited Warranty
While we’ve mostly focused on pre-owned BMWs, new BMWs can get extended warranties too. A lot of the same rules of thumb apply here – if you’re planning on keeping the car a while, it may benefit you to investigate your extended warranty options. Of course, the BMW New Vehicle Limited Warranty helps covers quite a lot on its own.
The New Vehicle Warranty covers manufacturing defects and workmanship flaws. Think of stuff along the lines of badly fitting trim panels or a seat adjuster switch that breaks off in your hand. You’ll enjoy four years and 50,000 miles of coverage. It also includes:
- Rust Perforation Warranty. BMW covers rust perforation for twelve years, with no mileage limit.
- Federal Emissions Warranty. All emissions related parts are covered for 2 years/24,000 miles, and specific control devices are covered for 8 years/80,000 miles. This is extended to 3 years/50,000 miles and 7 years/70,000 miles in California. Also limited to California: TZEV vehicles are covered for 15 years or 150,000 miles.
BMW Certified Pre-Owned Warranty
One of the leading reasons people buy pre-owned BMWs at all is BMW’s Certified Pre-Owned (CPO) Warranty. It’s largely similar to buying a brand new car – including carrying over the balance of the 4 year/50,000 mile New Vehicle Limited Warranty. But it goes even further than that.
The CPO warranty covers an additional 1 year/unlimited miles under the New Vehicle Limited warranty. Remember – this covers parts of the car that are considered manufacturing defects – not maintenance or wear and tear items.
Of course, not all vehicles are certifiable. Upon taking in a used BMW, a certified BMW dealership needs to conduct a thorough inspection, review the CARFAX or AutoCheck report, and ensure only BMW OEM parts are installed. All of this documentation is sent to BMW North America, and a fee is paid. Only after these steps can BMW North America certify the vehicle.
There are a handful of other perks when deciding to purchase a Certified Pre-Owned BMW. BMW Financial Services typically offers more competitive incentives and interest rates to Certified buyers. Naturally, BMW-supported extended service contracts are typically much more aggressively priced, as well.
Our Affiliate Partners at CARCHEX
CARCHEX
Founded in the late 1990s as a vehicle inspection service in Baltimore, Maryland, CARCHEX quickly became much more. Current CEO Jason Goldsmith saved a bunch of money by having CARCHEX inspect a vehicle he was considering purchasing; this helped him realize its value as a customer-facing service. He bought the assets of CARCHEX with the express desire to educate and assist potential buyers. CARCHEX became a leader in the service, and later expanded into the extended warranty field. CARCHEX has since become a trusted extended warranty service for thousands of customers.
FAQ: BMW Extended Warranty
Almost always, yes. If you plan to keep the car long term, you will likely save thousands of dollars with an extended warranty. The average cost to drive a BMW for one year is $1,000 – $1,700. That’s much more than most extended warranties will cost you, especially over a long period of time. Also, considering that a fuel pump replacement can cost between $1500 to $2750, then the need for a BMW Extended Warranty becomes obvious.
Most of the BMW Extended warranty costs between $3,000 and $4,000, but prices vary depending on coverage selected, the year of your BMW and its condition. Top tier Platinum Plans can cost more than $6,000 for a 5 year/100,000-mile. A BMW Gold Warranty can cost around $3,500 for a 7 year/75,000-mile.
Just like buying a car, you can negotiate the cost of a BMW extended warranty. BMW cars are expensive vehicles to maintain, so extended warranty is likely to be pricey as well.
Of course. You can buy a BMW extended warranty at a later date. In fact, you can buy BMW’s Ultimate Protection extended warranty anytime before your vehicle’s original factory warranty expires.
BMW’s New Vehicle Limited Warranty lasts four years or 50,000 miles. There are select parts that are covered longer. Maintenance is free; three years or 36,000 miles – but only at a BMW store.
Depending on your warranty, everything from regular maintenance to complicated engine repairs. But it depends on your provider and level of coverage. Consult your warranty documents or call a representative.

title: سيتروين 2CV الكهربائية تعود من جديد في 2026.. الأيقونة الفرنسية بسعر اقتصادي
author: Top Gear Middle East; محمد مكحل
text:
بعد عقود طويلة من حضورها كواحدة من أكثر السيارات الفرنسية ارتباطاً بالذاكرة الشعبية، تستعد سيتروين (Citroen) لإحياء اسم 2CV رسمياً ضمن مشروع كهربائي جديد يهدف إلى تقديم سيارة “مناسبة” التكلفة، عملية، وخفيفة “الروح”.. مع جرعة شخصية فرنسية يصعب تجاهلها..
جاء الإعلان عبر مجموعة ستيلانتيس (Stellantis) ضمن خطتها الصناعية الجديدة الممتدة حتى عام 2030. لتؤكد الشركة أن واحدة من أشهر سياراتها التاريخية في طريقها للعودة إلى الطرقات الأوروبية من جديد. لكن هذه المرة بصيغة كهربائية بالكامل، وفلسفة مصممة لتخاطب جيل حديث مختلف تماماً..
يحمل الخبر وزن خاص داخل أوروبا، لأن سيتروين 2CV لم تكن يوماً فئة عادية. منذ ظهورها الأول عام 1948، تحولت بسرعة إلى رمز اجتماعي وثقافي في فرنسا. سيارة بسيطة، خفيفة، عملية، وقادرة على الوصول إلى الناس قبل أن تفكر في إبهارهم بالأرقام والمواصفات. ولهذا السبب بالتحديد، أي محاولة لإعادة تقديمها اليوم تبدو أكبر بكثير من مجرد إطلاق طراز جديد داخل السوق.
وصف اكزافيير تشاردون، الرئيس التنفيذي لسيتروين، المشروع بأنه من أكبر تحديات العلامة حالياً، موضحاً أن النسخة الجديدة ستحمل الجوهر الذي جعل 2CV مرتبطة بالناس: الحرية، سهولة الاستخدام، والطابع المختلف عن كل ما يدور حولها.
ومن الواضح أن العلامة تتعامل مع المشروع بعقلية مختلفة عن موجة “الريترو” المعتادة في الصناعة حالياً. لا تعتمد الفكرة هنا على استنساخ التصميم القديم حرفياً، ولا على صناعة نسخة كلاسيكية كهربائية للحنين فقط.. التوجه أقرب إلى إعادة تفسير لفلسفة “العنوان” نفسه بلغة حديثة تناسب واقع 2026 وما بعده.
في هذا السياق، لم تكشف سيتروين حتى الآن عن تفاصيل تقنية دقيقة، لكن المؤكد أن الصيغة الجديدة ستكون كهربائية بالكامل، مع موعد أوضح للكشف عنها خلال أكتوبر 2026. السيناريو الأقرب؟ مركبة مدمجة مخصصة للمدن الأوروبية، تعتمد على منصة كهربائية حديثة من عائلة STLA One التابعة لستيلانتيس، مع تركيز كبير على الوزن المنخفض، الكفاءة، وسهولة الاستخدام اليومية داخل المدن والضواحي.
وهذا تحديداً ما يجعل المشروع مثيراً. يعيش السوق الأوروبي اليوم مرحلة حساسة جداً. الأسعار ترتفع، والسيارات الكهربائية الجديدة تتجه أكثر فأكثر نحو التكنولوجيا المكلفة والفئات الأعلى سعراً. وبين هذا المشهد، بدأت الحاجة تظهر بوضوح لسيارات كهربائية عملية وسهلة الوصول لشريحة أكبر من الناس. ومن هنا تبدو عودة 2CV منطقية جداً. أليس كذلك يا صديقي؟ نعم!
فكرة سيارة كهربائية صغيرة، خفيفة، ذات شخصية مميزة، وسعر محسوب بعناية.. قد تمنح سيتروين نقطة قوة مهمة داخل معركة السيارات الأوروبية القادمة، خصوصاً مع المنافسة المتصاعدة من الشركات الصينية، وعودة أسماء تاريخية مثل رينو 5 وأوبل فرونتيرا بصيغ جديدة.
ويبقى السؤال الأكبر الذي يشغل الجمهور حالياً:
“كيف ستبدو 2CV الجديدة؟”..
“هل تتجه سيتروين نحو تصميم يحافظ على الخطوط الناعمة والانحناءات الشهيرة؟”..
“أم تفاجئ الجميع بكروس أوفر مدمجة تحمل الاسم فقط؟”..
لا تزال أمام الإجابة الكاملة بضعة أشهر..
لكن شيء واحد يبدو واضح من الآن:
“سيتروين قررت إعادة واحدة من أهم شخصياتها التاريخية إلى المسرح.. والمشهد الأوروبي ينتظر بشغف كبير ما ستقدمه العلامة الفرنسية هذه المرة”..

title: 2023 BMW M3 - Buyer's Guide, Pricing and Specs
author: Horatiu Boeriu
text:
Table of contents
2023 BMW M3 Overview
The sixth-generation M3 debuted as a 2021 model, and it’s a bit of a departure from the previous generations in terms of performance and styling. It marks the first generation of the M3 with available all-wheel drive, the first to receive a true automatic transmission (instead of a dual-clutch unit or sequential manual gearbox), and offers some seriously cool performance options, like high-bolstered carbon fiber bucket seats. For the 2023 BMW M3 models, a manual transmission is offered only in rear-wheel drive configurations and receives less power than its all-wheel drive brethren, but we suspect that won’t matter to die-hard manual enthusiasts.
BMW M3 Engine, Transmission, and Performance
The standard M3 has a six-speed manual transmission and a twin-turbocharged inline six-cylinder engine, internally designated as the S58. It generates 473 horsepower and 406 pound-feet of torque and can pull off a zero to 60 mph time of about four seconds. The Competition trim bumps power up to 503 horsepower and 479 pound-feet of torque, a noticeable increase from the driver’s seat. Add xDrive all-wheel drive to drop that zero-to-sixty time to three and a half seconds or less. All xDrive-equipped M3 sedans are Competition cars, and there’s no manual available for any Competition trim vehicles. As expected, there are tons of performance options available for the BMW M3 – like carbon ceramic brakes and M Drive Professional, which features ten-stage traction control.
Fuel Economy and MPG
The 2023 BMW M3 is currently rated at 16 city and 23 highway MPG, for a combined figure of 19 MPG. That’s probably a fair representation of what you’ll achieve, but driving the M3 hard is where it shines and will quickly shrink those numbers. Its 15.6-gallon tank will allow for around 300 miles of range, more if it’s highway-heavy.
Interior and Cargo Space
The cabin of the M3 is classic BMW – minimalist and practical, with premium materials. Extended Merino leather upholstery comes standard, and you can add a Full leather package that adds leather on the lower half of the dashboard, door panels, and parts of the center console. A very pretty carbon fiber roof comes standard, but you can opt for a moonroof for no charge. As far as space goes, the M3 is a true-blue five-seater with 35.6 inches of rear leg room. A 13 cubic feet trunk has plenty of space for luggage or bags and the rear seats fold down for even more space.
BMW M3 Technology and Connectivity
For 2022, the M3 receives iDrive 8, and a curved display lifted straight out of vehicles like the BMW i4 and iX. 2021 models are stuck with iDrive 7 and a 12.3-inch touchscreen, but that isn’t all that bad considering it retains physical climate control adjustments. Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are standard no matter which model year you’re looking for, and so are staples like navigation and MyBMW app integration. A configurable, fully digital gauge cluster comes standard. A heads-up display is not standard but comes with the value-packed Executive Package, which also adds remote engine start, a heated steering wheel, a power tailgate, and more.
Safety and Driver Assistance Features
The 2023 BMW M3 comes standard with driver aids like frontal collision warning, blind-spot monitoring, and lane-departure warning. Optional extras include radar-assisted adaptive cruise control and a surround-view camera system that allows the BMW M3 to self-park.
BMW M3 Pricing
The base M3 (six-speed manual) starts at $74,300. The 2023 BMW M3 Competition starts at $78,600, and adding xDrive brings the base MSRP up to $82,600. Used examples are beginning to pop up but don’t expect to save a ton of money, as demand is still high. However, as this current generation ages, prices should start falling, and we’ll keep this page updated with the latest info.
2023 BMW M3 FAQ
The BMW M3 Model Year 2023 is available to order now. There are no major changes from the 2022 BMW M3 model, other than a new large curved display and the addition of iDrive 8.
Even though the M3 has yet to receive the facelift treatment, it does have a major novelty for 2023 by also switching to the Operating System 8. It comes as standard and pairs a 12.3-inch digital driver’s display with a 14.9-inch touchscreen for the infotainment.
Absolutely! Despite having a controversial exterior design, the G80 BMW M3 sedan is one of the best driving M cars in decades. Not only it brings an all-wheel drive system with over 500 horsepower, but it can also be order with a six-speed manual and rear-wheel drive.
The value of a BMW M3 decreases over the years, similar to other BMWs and sportscars. Expect a BMW M3 sedan to hang on to 55-60 percent of its original value on average. The BMW M3 has a great branding name attached to it and a loyal following, so they will always be in demand.

title: فورد إسكورت Mk1 RS 2026 الجديدة: عودة الأسطورة بمحرك 10,000 دورة وسعر يتجاوز 467 ألف دولار
author: Top Gear Middle East; محمد مكحل
text:
حسناً، سنبدأ مقالتنا هذه المرة بسؤال محوري: “هل نحن أمام أعظم فورد إسكورت (Ford Escort) في التاريخ؟”. نعم، هناك أسماء لا تموت مهما مرت العقود. أسماء ترتبط بذكريات الحلبات، وطرق الريف البريطانية، وأيام كانت فيها المتعة الميكانيكية تُقاس بخفة الوزن ونقاء التجربة أكثر من عدد الشاشات أو أنظمة المساعدة الإلكترونية.
ومن بين تلك الأسماء، تقف فورد إسكورت Mk1 في مكانة خاصة داخل ذاكرة عشاق القيادة. لتعود الأسطورة الآن إلى الحياة بصورة لم يتوقعها أحد، كمشروع يحمل اسم “Ford Escort Mk1 RS” الجديدة من Boreham Motorworks، بعد أن حصل على اعتماد رسمي من فورد، وأُعيد تطويره بالكامل من الصفر ليجمع بين روح الماضي وأحدث تقنيات الهندسة الحديثة. والنتيجة؟ آلة قيادة تبدو وكأنها خرجت من سباقات السبعينيات، بعد أن أمضت سنوات طويلة داخل مختبر هندسي فائق التطور..
ليست إعادة ترميم.. وليست سيارة تنبعث مجدداً من الماضي الآثر.. من الصعب وضع هذا المشروع داخل تصنيف واحد. فهو لا ينتمي إلى عالم Restomod التقليدي، كما لا يمكن اعتباره إعادة إحياء “Continuation Car” بنسخة تحاكي الأصل حرفياً. لقد اختارت Boreham Motorworks مسار مختلف بالكامل..
بدأت الفكرة من إرث Ford Escort Group 5 التابعة لفريق Alan Mann Racing، وهي صاحبة الإنجاز الأيقوني بتحقيق بطولة سيارات الصالون عام 1968، ثم أُعيدت صياغة كل التفاصيل تقريباً لتولد شخصية جديدة تحمل روح الماضي مع أداء معاصر. وبصراحة؟ قد تكون هذه أكثر إسكورت تطوراً وتعقيداً من الناحية الهندسية منذ ظهور الاسم لأول مرة..
الرقم الذي يجذب الانتباه مباشرةً هو الوزن. تزن الصيغة الجديدة 895 كجم فقط. وعندما تقترن هذه الكتلة الخفيفة بمحرك يولد 325 حصان، تصبح النتيجة مذهلة. تبلغ نسبة القوة إلى الوزن 363 حصان لكل طن. وللمقارنة فقط.. تحقق بورشه 911 GT3 حوالي 355 حصان لكل طن. نعم.. يتفوق هذا الطرح الصغير على واحدة من أشهر أيقونات القيادة في العالم “على الورق”..
ماذا عن الأداء؟ هنا تنطلق الحبكة الروائية الميكانيكية بكامل حقيقتها! المحرك القياسي عبارة عن وحدة Twin Cam بسعة 1.8 لتر وقوة 182 حصان. لكن اختار معظم العملاء الخيار الذي يحمل اسم TEN-K. ونستطيع تفهّم السبب بسهولة. نحن نتحدث عن محرك جديد بالكامل بسعة 2.15 لتر وأربع أسطوانات مستقيمة وتنفس طبيعي بالكامل. تم تطويره باستخدام تقنيات تصنيع متقدمة تشمل قوالب مطبوعة بتقنية ثلاثية الأبعاد لتقليل الكتلة إلى 85 كجم فقط.
ويحمل مواصفات أقرب إلى عالم السباقات.. رأس أسطوانات 16 صمام.. بوابات سحب مستقلة.. نظام تزييت Dry Sump.. عمود مرفق مصنع من قطعة معدنية واحدة.. وهندسة منافذ وصمامات مستوحاة من الفورمولا 1.. أما الأرقام؟ 325 حصان دون أي شاحن توربو. وعند تقسيم القوة على السعة نحصل على 155 حصان لكل لتر..
يتجاوز هذا الرقم ما تحققه فيراري 458 سبيشالي (Ferrari 458 Speciale)، بل يتفوق حتى على أستون مارتن فالكيري (Aston Martin Valkyrie) من حيث كثافة القوة لكل لتر. والأجمل؟ يقف الخط الأحمر الفاصل عند 10,000 دورة في الدقيقة. رقم اعتادت عليه محركات السباقات أكثر من الطرق العامة.. أليس كذلك يا صديقي؟
ورغم التشابه البصري مع Escort الكلاسيكية، فإن البنية الهندسية مختلفة جذرياً. تمت إعادة تصميم الإطار الأمامي بالكامل مع زيادة قاعدة العجلات بمقدار 30 ملم. كما ارتفعت الصلابة الهيكلية بنسبة 50%.
وفي الخلف حصل المحور على عملية إعادة هندسة شاملة خفضت وزنه إلى النصف تقريباً مقارنةً بالمكون الأصلي القريب من حيّز 100 كجم. جرى تحقيق ذلك عبر استخدام مركز من الألمنيوم وأنابيب محور مصنوعة من التيتانيوم. أما غطاء المحرك والباب الخلفي فعُمِل على تصنيعهما من ألياف الكربون لتقليل الكتلة أكثر.
لا يقتصر الأمر عند هذا الحد. فإذا كان المحرك مثير للإعجاب، فإن منظومة التعليق تكشف حجم الطموح الكامن خلف المشروع. جُهّزت السيارة بمخمدات R53 القابلة للتعديل ثنائي الاتجاه. هل يبدو السم مألوف لك؟ إنها نفس الشركة التي تزود Gordon Murray Automotive بمكونات التعليق المستخدمة في T.50 الشهيرة. وهذا وحده كافٍ لإدراك مستوى التطوير الحاصلة عليه هذه الأيقونة البريطانية.
تم ربط المحرك بقير Holinger يدوي من خمس نسب. ويعتمد تخطيط Dogleg التقليدي حين تأتي السرعة الأولى في موضع مختلف عن المعتاد، مع نسب قصيرة وحادة التركيز على الأداء. أما عصا التبديل فتقع بالقرب من المقود بشكل يمنح شعور ميكانيكي مباشر يذكرنا بعصر كانت فيه العلاقة بين السائق والآلة أكثر قرباً من أي وقت مضى.. حتى نظام التوجيه الكهربائي وُثّق ببرمجة خاصة لتقليل المساعدة تدريجياً مع ارتفاع السرعة بهدف تعزيز الإحساس بالطريق.
في الداخل، اختفت بساطة إسكورت القديمة لتحل مكانها بيئة تحمل مستوى تشطيب أقرب إلى إصدارات الإنتاج المحدود. جلود ناعمة عالية الجودة. ألواح أبواب من ألياف الكربون. لوحة عدادات مصممة خصيصاً لهذا المشروع. مفاتيح تحكم جديدة بالكامل. اتصال بالهواتف الذكية. وقفص حماية مصنوع من الكربون. ورغم كل هذه الإضافات، ما زالت المقصورة تحتفظ بروحها الكلاسيكية بصورة رائعة.
في حين، وكلما اقتربت من الهيكل، بدأت تكتشف حجم العمل المُنجز. صيغت معظم الأجزاء المعدنية الخارجية من الألمنيوم المشغول بدقة عالية لمقابض الأبواب، وأغطية المرايا، وطبعاً تفاصيل الزخارف. يوفر كل عنصر إحساس أقرب إلى عالم السوبركارز منه إلى إرث إسكورت الشعبي المعروف من الجميع..
سيقتصر الإنتاج على 150 نسخة فقط. أما السعر فيبدأ من 467 ألف دولار قبل الخيارات الإضافية. ومع اختيار محرك TEN-K وبعض التجهيزات الخاصة، من السهل أن تتخطّى الفاتورة النهائية حاجز الـ 500 ألف دولار وربما أكثر.. رقم قد يبدو صادم عندما نتحدث عن عنوان مثل “إسكورت”. لكن الحقيقة أن هذا المشروع كسر حدود الاسم منذ فترة طويلة..
في نهاية المطاف، يبرز سؤال واحد لا يحمل التأويل بأكثر من خيار.. هل ما زالت هذه السيارة تُعتبر فورد إسكورت فقط؟
نعم.. من ناحية الروح.
أما في ما يتعلّق بالهندسة والتقنيات ومستوى التطوير، فنحن أمام مشروع مختلف تماماً عما عرفناه سابقاً.
وزن فائق الخفة.
محرك تنفس طبيعي يدور حتى 10,000 دورة بالدقيقة.
دفع خلفي.
قير يدوي.
وتفاصيل هندسية تجعل كثيراً من السيارات الخارقة تبدو أقل تميزاً على الورق.
قد يرى البعض أن السعر ابتعد كثيراً عن الجذور التاريخية.
لكن إذا نجحت Boreham Motorworks في ترجمة هذه الأرقام إلى تجربة قيادة استثنائية، فقد تدخل هذه التحفة نادي أعظم سيارات الطرقات الجبلية في العصر الحديث.
وعندها…. ستكون فورد قد استعادت إحدى أساطيرها بطريقة لم يتوقعها أحد.

title: 2023 BMW i4: Review, Price, Specs and Range
author: Horatiu Boeriu
text:
Table of contents
BMW i4 Overview
The 2023 BMW i4 is a massively important car for the Bavarian brand. Not only is it BMW’s first electric sedan but it’s also its current entry-level electric vehicles, making it the electric BMW that most customers will buy. If it’s a great car, it will be a massive hit among BMW customers. BMW’s ability to take on Tesla and Lucid rides on the BMW i4’s success, so BMW needs it to do well. If you’re interesting in putting a BMW i4 in your driveway or garage, there are a few things you should know. So let’s break down the 2022 BMW i4 Gran Coupe so you know what to get when you buy one.
Price for BMW i4 Models
The most important thing that matter is price — can I afford the BMW i4? There are two models current offered by BMW; the entry-level BMW i4 eDrive40 and the high-performance BMW i4 M50. The former starts at $55,400, while the latter starts at $$65,900.
For the BMW i4 eDrive40, an M Sport package, which brings 19″ wheels, Shadowline black exterior trim, and an M Sport steering wheel; costs $2,400. If you want an upgraded paint color, it costs $550, but if you want an especially cool color, it’ll cost you $1,500. There are three different standard interior options but if you want an upgrade, it will cost you $1,450.
However, for the BMW i4 M50, it lacks an M Sport package, due to the fact that it’s already an M Performance car. You can still get Shadowline black trim, though, to black out the Cerium grey highlights.
Another exciting electric BMW coming in 2023 is the BMW i4 eDrive35. The entry-level i4 uses a single electrically-excited synchronous motor delivering 281 horsepower and 295 lb-ft of torque sent to the rear wheels. BMW estimates a 0 to 60 mph time of just 5.8 seconds.
The BMW i4 eDrive35 is powered by high-voltage batteries with an energy content of 70.2 kWh gross and 66 kWh net. When fitted with the standard 18-inch aero wheels, the i4 eDrive35 is expected to deliver an EPA range of about 260 miles (estimated range of up to 260 miles according to preliminary BMW AG tests based on the EPA’s test procedure standards).
Utilizing DC fast charging, the batteries can be charged at a rate of up to 180 kW and, based on early testing, owners can expect to be able to charge the HV battery from 10% to 80% in only 32 minutes.
Release Date
Both the 2023 BMW i4 40 and i4 M50 are available to order in the US market. While I’m not sure which models are/aren’t available in all markets, both are now available to order in Europe as well. Deliveries for the BMW i4 will begin March 2022 in the US.
Electric Range for BMW i4 Models
Despite having different prices, power, and motor count, both the BMW i4 eDrive40 and i4 M50 have the same battery pack, a 83.9 kWh gross battery, with 81.5 kWh net. The less powerful BMW i4 40, with its single rear-mounted electric motor, makes 335 horsepower. If you opt for the more powerful BMW i4 M50, you get two electric motors, one at each axle, and 536 horsepower. BMW i4 eDrive40 has an EPA range of 301 miles when equipped with 18-inch wheels and 282 miles when equipped with 19-inch wheels. The more powerful and M-tuned BMW i4 M50 is rated on the EPA range at 270 miles when equipped with 19-inch wheels and 227 miles when equipped with 20-inch wheels.
Both cars have a max charging speed of 200 kW, which allows the BMW i4 40 to add another 102 miles of range to its battery in just ten minutes. As for the i4 M50, ten minutes gets you 87 miles.
Infotainment System And Technology
The 2023 BMW i4 come with iDrive 8 and a brand new digital instrument cluster and an infotainment screen. The curved display is composed of two separate screens measuring 14.9 inches and 12.3 inches, respectively. The standard head-up display is integrated flush into the surface of the instrument panel. Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are also standard in the BMW i4. Interior tech also includes a standard 10-speaker sound system. An optional 16-speaker Harman Kardon audio system is available.
Should I Buy a BMW i4?
If you want one, then you should probably order one now. The first batch of BMW i4 units set for the US has already sold out. So if you want one, you’re going to have to get in on the second round of production, so you’re going to want to order as soon as possible.
The 2023 BMW i4 Drive35 comes with a manufacturer’s suggested retail price (MSRP) of $51,400, plus a destination charge.
The 2023 i4 eDrive40 starts at $59,899 and the 2023 BMW i4 M50 is $67,300. There’s a change of rules in 2023 regarding which electric vehicles qualify for a $7,500 federal tax credit. The 2023 BMW i4 do not qualify for the tax credit. BMW also includes two years of free 30-minute charging sessions using the Electrify America network.
State incentives might apply. For example, New York’s Drive Clean Rebate scheme offers $500.
BMW i4 FAQ
Deliveries of the i4 started in March 2022. Delivery times may vary dependent on when your pre-order was placed and when your vehicle has been configured with your selected BMW Center. But definitely expect at least a few weeks of wait time for a new BMW i4.
The new IRA law eliminates tax credits for vehicles not assembled in North America, including the BMW i4.
BMW i4 takes pride in offering a design that look similar to the regular BMW 4 Series. Also, starting at $51,400, the BMW i4 offers a great value for the money. And if you buy the BMW i4 M50, then you’re getting top performance worthy of an M car.
You can’t charge your BMW i4 at a Tesla Supercharger.
S customers who buy a 2022 BMW i4 or BMW iX will get two years of free 30-minute charging from Electrify America.
The BMW i4 eDrive35 has 260 miles of EPA range, while the i4 eDrive40 has an estimated 300 miles of driving range. The BMW i4 M50’s estimated driving range is 270 miles.
2023 BMW i4
Good
- Good electric driving range
- A familiar BMW design
- A premium interior and materials
Bad
- Oversized kidney grille
- Expensive when fully loaded
- Doesn't qualify for federal tax credits
